summary: This part of the Privacy Enhanced Mail series defines the cryptographic algorithms, usage modes, and identifiers used to support PEM, with formats and references. It is historic.

plainLanguage.summary: The locking tools used for secret mail need exact names and settings. This paper lists them so every mail program means the same thing. It is historic.

subtitle: The list of ciphers, digests and key formats that Privacy Enhanced Mail was allowed to use, with the exact names and byte layouts.

tldr.problem: The Privacy Enhanced Mail (PEM) documents needed a precise, replaceable list of cryptographic algorithms, modes and identifiers so that every implementation meant the same thing.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 1423 names DES in CBC mode for message encryption, RSA-MD2 and RSA-MD5 for integrity checks, DES-ECB and DES-EDE for symmetric key management, and RSA for asymmetric keys, with their header strings, parameters and formats.
tldr.outcome: It was a standards-track RFC that replaced RFC 1115. It is now Historic.

today: RFC 1423 is Historic. It obsoleted RFC 1115, and no later RFC is listed as obsoleting or updating it. It was written to be read together with RFC 1421, RFC 1422 and RFC 1424.

sections.title: What This Part of PEM Covers
sections.content:
RFC 1423 is Part III of the Privacy Enhancement for Internet Electronic Mail series. It gives definitions, formats, references and citations for the cryptographic algorithms, usage modes, identifiers and parameters used by Privacy Enhanced Mail (PEM). It replaces RFC 1115.

The material is split into four areas: message encryption, message integrity check algorithms, symmetric key management and asymmetric key management. The authors kept it in a separate document because parts of it may be changed, added or replaced without affecting the RFCs that cite it. Other algorithms would need case-by-case study and might be documented first in Prototype or Experimental RFCs.
sections.plainLanguage: The main mail-privacy rules stay put, while this separate paper lists the actual locks. That way the list can change without rewriting everything else.

sections.title: Message Encryption with DES-CBC
sections.content:
Only one message encryption algorithm is defined: the Data Encryption Standard (DES) in Cipher Block Chaining (CBC) mode. The string DES-CBC in an encapsulated PEM header marks it. It encrypts the message text and, with asymmetric key management, the message signature.

Input is padded to a multiple of 8 octets by appending between 1 and 8 octets, each holding the number of octets added. The key is 64 bits, of which 56 are used and 8 are odd parity bits. A new pseudorandom key and a new 64-bit Initialization Vector (IV) shall be generated for every ENCRYPTED PEM message.

The DEK-Info: header carries exactly two arguments: the string DES-CBC and the IV as 16 ASCII hexadecimal digits. The RFC also fixes the octet ordering of a key when it is fed into another process such as RSA, so that all implementations agree.
sections.plainLanguage: The message is scrambled in chunks of 8 bytes, and each chunk depends on the one before. The scrambling uses a fresh secret key and starting value every time, and the starting value travels with the message.

sections.title: Message Integrity Check Algorithms
sections.content:
A Message Integrity Check (MIC) is a digest that lets the receiver detect changes to a message. Two algorithms are defined: RSA-MD2, computed as in RFC 1319, and RSA-MD5, computed as in RFC 1321. Each takes a message of any length and yields a 16-octet value, and each has an ASN.1 object identifier.

A compliant PEM implementation shall be able to process both on incoming messages, and the sender chooses which one to use. With symmetric key management the 16-octet MIC is split into two 8-octet halves, each encrypted on its own, and shown as 32 hexadecimal digits in the fourth argument of the Key-Info: header.

The RFC also notes an error in the text of RFC 1319, Section 3.2, and says the C source code in that RFC's appendix is correct.
sections.plainLanguage: A digest is like a short fingerprint of the whole message. If even one letter changes, the fingerprint no longer matches, so the reader knows something was altered.

sections.title: Symmetric and Asymmetric Key Management
sections.content:
With symmetric key management the message key (the DEK) and the MIC are encrypted under a shared key using DES. DES-ECB (Electronic Codebook mode) must be supported by any implementation that supports symmetric key management. DES-EDE, the Encrypt-Decrypt-Encrypt mode from ANSI X9.17, is optional.

With asymmetric key management, PEM uses RSA keys. The public exponent must be either 65537 or 3, with 3 encouraged for fast certificate checks, and the modulus may be from 508 to 1024 bits. Two object identifiers may name an RSA key in a certificate: rsa from X.509 and rsaEncryption from PKCS #1. Implementations must accept both.

RSAEncryption from PKCS #1 encrypts DEKs and MICs. A DEK uses PKCS #1 block type 02 with random non-zero padding. A MIC uses block type 01 with padding of 0xFF octets and is ASN.1 encoded together with its digest algorithm. All PEM implementations supporting asymmetric key management shall support it. Certificates and CRLs are signed with md2WithRSAEncryption, which combines RSA-MD2 and RSAEncryption.
sections.plainLanguage: The message's secret key has to travel safely. Either both sides already share a secret, or the sender locks it with the receiver's public padlock that only the receiver can open.

sections.title: The Descriptive Grammar
sections.content: The final section is an addendum to the PEM BNF using RFC 822 notation. It lists the official identifiers: DES-CBC for message encryption, DES-EDE, DES-ECB and RSA for key management, RSA for signatures and RSA-MD2 or RSA-MD5 for the MIC. It also defines the IV as 16 hexadecimal characters, a symmetrically encrypted DEK as 16 hexadecimal characters and a symmetrically encrypted MIC as two blocks of 16. It imports hexchar and encbin from RFC 1421.
sections.plainLanguage: This part spells out, letter by letter, the exact words and shapes a PEM header may contain, like a form with fixed boxes.

sections.title: Patents and Security
sections.content: The Security Considerations section is one sentence: this entire document is about security. A separate patent statement says this version of PEM relies on patented public key technology. It names the patents that Public Key Partners held sub-licensing rights to and says PKP gave written assurance of reasonable, nondiscriminatory terms. The Internet Society and related bodies take no position on the validity or scope of those patents.
sections.plainLanguage: The paper says the whole thing is about keeping secrets. It also warns that some of the locking tricks were owned by a company, which promised to let people use them for a fair price.

items.label: Message encryption
items.desc: DES in Cipher Block Chaining mode, the only message encryption algorithm defined.

items.label: Symmetric key management
items.desc: Must be supported when symmetric key management is used.

items.label: Asymmetric key management
items.desc: RSAEncryption from PKCS #1 for DEKs and MICs; also used for signatures.
